result: C. elegans was the first multicellular organism in which genetic code expansion was established, with ncAA incorporation demonstrated in multiple tissues.
evaluation: Claims C1 and C2 are supported by citations to prior work (Greiss and Chin, 2011; Parrish et al., 2012), establishing the historical context for genetic code expansion in C. elegans.

result: Nuclear export sequences (NES) can relocalize PylRS from the nucleus to the cytoplasm in eukaryotic cells. The S-NES successfully shifted PCKRS localization from nuclear to cytoplasmic, and all tested NES variants achieved nuclear export.
evaluation: Claims C3-C7 are supported by established knowledge (C3), prior work citation (C4), and experimental data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B (C5-C7). The localization data directly demonstrates the predicted effect of NES addition.

result: Different NES variants differentially affect ncAA incorporation efficiency. The PKIα-NES and Smad4-NES robustly increased PCK incorporation efficiency, while p120cts-NES reduced it. The optimized tRNA variant C15 significantly increased incorporation efficiency, with the Smad4-NES::PCKRS/tRNA(C15) and PKIα-NES::PCKRS/tRNA(C15) pairs improving incorporation efficiency by more than 50-fold (from <0.1% to 4.6% and 4.4%, respectively).
evaluation: Claims C8-C11 are supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2C, E, F, G and supplementary figures. The quantitative improvement (>50-fold) is directly measured and reported with appropriate controls. The data clearly demonstrate differential effects of NES variants and the synergistic improvement with tRNA(C15).

result: Cre recombinase can be photocaged by replacing K201 with PCK, and PC-Cre has previously been expressed in mammalian cell culture and zebrafish embryos.
evaluation: Claims C12 and C13 are supported by citations to prior work (Gibb et al., 2010; Luo et al., 2016; Brown et al., 2018b) and illustrated in Figure 3A and B. This establishes the foundation for the photocaged Cre approach.

result: Using the optimized Smad4-NES::PCKRS/tRNA(C15) system, PC-Cre photoactivation resulted in target gene expression in 63% of animals 24 hr after uncaging, with no expression without UV treatment. This represents a vast improvement over the 1% observed with unmodified PCKRS and tRNA(Pyl).
evaluation: Claims C14-C16 are supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D. The 63-fold improvement in activation efficiency is clearly demonstrated with appropriate controls (no UV treatment showing no expression). Statistical significance is indicated in the figure.

result: The improved Smad4-NES::PCKRS/tRNA(C15) incorporation system produces 4-5% full-length protein. The optimized PC-Cre (optPC-Cre) significantly improved target gene activation from 63% to 97% compared to non-optimized PC-Cre.
evaluation: Claims C17 and C18 are supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2F and 3D. The improvement from 63% to 97% activation is substantial and statistically significant. However, the 4-5% full-length protein production suggests that the majority of translation still terminates at the amber codon, which is acknowledged by the authors.

result: OptPC-Cre enables optical control of neuronal activity through ChR2 expression. No ChR2::mKate2 expression was observed without PCK or UV activation. Blue light activation of ChR2-expressing neurons induced reversals in the presence of ATR but not in its absence. The strongest responses were seen with optPC-Cre, while animals with unmodified PCKRS showed almost no response.
evaluation: Claims C19-C24 are supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3D, F, G and supplementary figures, plus Videos 1 and 2. The behavioral assays demonstrate functional optogenetic control with appropriate controls (no PCK, no UV, no ATR). The comparison between different Cre variants shows clear improvement with optimization.

result: C. elegans has six mechanosensory neurons for soft touch perception (AVM, ALML, ALMR, PVM, PLML, PLMR). Worms respond with backward movement to anterior touch and forward movement to posterior touch. Optogenetic activation of anterior neurons (AVM/ALM) results in reversals, while activation of posterior neurons (PVM/PLM) results in forward movement. Concurrent activation of all six neurons results in reversals in most cases, and repeated activation leads to habituation.
evaluation: Claims C25-C30 are supported by established knowledge about C. elegans mechanosensory neurons (C25), citations to prior work (C26, C30), and inference from previous studies (C27-C29). This provides the biological context for the subsequent experiments.

result: LaserTAC enables cell-specific gene activation. After 12-24 hr, Chrimson::mKate2 expression was only present in laser-targeted cells. Selective activation of optPC-Cre in both PLM neurons or in PLML/PLMR individually was achieved. The presence of the PCK incorporation machinery and optPC-Cre did not affect touch sensory neuron function.
evaluation: Claims C31-C33 are supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4C-E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D. The spatial specificity of activation is clearly demonstrated, and the control experiments (touch assays) confirm that the system does not interfere with normal neuronal function.

result: Optogenetic stimulation of PLM neurons expressing Chrimson::mKate2 triggers forward movement. Animals expressing Chrimson in both PLM neurons (2PLM) showed robust responses, while mock-treated animals showed no response. Animals expressing Chrimson in only PLML or PLMR also showed clear reactions. All three expression patterns showed gradual reduction in response with repeated stimulation, consistent with habituation. The 2PLM animals responded more strongly than animals expressing Chrimson in either PLML or PLMR alone.
evaluation: Claims C34-C38 are supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5A,B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, and Videos 3-6. The behavioral responses are quantified with appropriate statistical analysis (two-way ANOVA). The habituation observation is consistent with prior work (Stirman et al., 2011).

result: PLML and PLMR show asymmetric connectivity within the C. elegans nervous system. PLMR forms chemical synapses to 10 downstream neurons including AVA and AVD, and gap junctions to PVCR, PHCR, and LUAR. PLML is connected exclusively through gap junctions to PVCL, PHCL, and LUAL, and forms no chemical synapses except a single connection to HSNL.
evaluation: Claims C39-C42 are based on established knowledge about the C. elegans connectome. This anatomical information is well-documented in the literature and provides the structural basis for interpreting the functional experiments.

result: Prior ablation studies showed that ablating both PLM neurons or PLMR alone increased backward movement in response to tap stimulus, while ablating PLML had no effect.
evaluation: Claims C43 and C44 are supported by citation to prior work (Wicks and Rankin, 1995). This provides historical context for the asymmetric function of PLML and PLMR.

result: Weak stimulation (0.1 s, 3 mW/cm²) was sufficient to elicit a response in animals expressing Chrimson in both PLMs, but neither PLML nor PLMR animals reacted individually. This indicates a synergistic effect of PLML and PLMR and the requirement for activation of both neurons to elicit a reaction in response to weak stimuli.
evaluation: Claims C45-C47 are supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5D-F and Figure 5—figure supplement 2. The synergistic effect (C47) is a reasonable inference from the observation that neither neuron alone responds to weak stimulation but both together do. However, alternative explanations (e.g., threshold effects) are not explicitly ruled out.

result: At higher illumination intensities, PLMR animals showed robust reactions at 14 mW/cm² and higher, while PLML animals consistently showed weaker responses than PLMR or 2PLM animals. Only at the highest intensity (74 mW/cm²) did all three expression patterns respond robustly. The observed differences are not due to differential Chrimson::mKate2 expression but are likely due to asymmetric connectivity of the two neurons.
evaluation: Claims C48-C52 are supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5D-F and Figure 5—figure supplements 2-3. The control for expression levels (C51, Figure 5—figure supplement 3) strengthens the conclusion that connectivity differences explain the functional asymmetry (C52). The inference about connectivity (C52) is reasonable given the anatomical data.

result: PLML and PLMR show some redundancy in triggering the tail touch response after strong stimulation. However, using weaker stimuli, only stimulation of both neurons elicits a response, indicative of a synergistic rather than simply redundant role. The results demonstrate asymmetric contributions of PLML and PLMR to the touch response.
evaluation: Claims C53-C55 are supported by experimental observations from the intensity-response experiments. The distinction between redundancy (at high intensity) and synergy (at low intensity) is well-supported by the data. The asymmetric contributions are clearly demonstrated.

result: A model is proposed where the touch response is controlled by two parallel pathways: (1) a gap junction pathway involving direct connections of both PLM neurons to PVC interneurons, which activate AVB and inhibit AVA/AVD to trigger forward motion; and (2) a chemical synapse pathway involving PLMR transmission to AVA/AVD to inhibit backward locomotion. When only PLMR is stimulated, both pathways are activated (stronger response), whereas PLML stimulation activates only the gap junction pathway (weaker response). The PVCs may act as electrical sinks for PLM signals. Stimulation of both PLM neurons results in full activation of both pathways. The strong synergistic effect indicates a requirement for stimulation of both PVC neurons.
evaluation: Claims C56-C65 present a mechanistic model inferred from experimental results and knowledge of the connectome. The model is consistent with the observed data (differential responses of PLML vs. PLMR, synergistic effect of both neurons) and the known anatomical connectivity. However, this is a proposed model that has not been directly tested through additional manipulations (e.g., PVC-specific perturbations). The model is reasonable and well-supported by the available evidence, but alternative explanations cannot be completely ruled out. The speculation about PVCs as electrical sinks (C63) is acknowledged as such.

result: C. elegans contains 302 neurons with determined physical connectivity. Two-thirds of neurons exist in bilaterally symmetric pairs.
evaluation: Claims C66-C68 are based on established knowledge and supported by citation to prior work (White et al., 1986). This provides general context for the study.

result: The optimized ncAA incorporation system will enable introduction of diverse chemical functionalities into proteins in C. elegans and is expected to be easily exportable to other organisms.
evaluation: Claims C69 and C70 are speculative about future applications. While C69 is supported by citations to prior work demonstrating various applications of ncAA incorporation, the actual implementation in C. elegans remains to be demonstrated. C70 is speculative about exportability, though the reasoning (based on non-organism-specific components) is sound. These are reasonable expectations but not demonstrated results.

result: C. elegans has evolved natural surveillance mechanisms to mitigate stop codon read-through, which should mitigate potential effects of the amber suppression system. The function of mechanosensory neurons is unaffected by the presence of the orthogonal ncAA incorporation machinery.
evaluation: Claim C71 is supported by citation to prior work (Arribere et al., 2016). Claim C72 is supported by experimental observation (touch assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D). Together, these address potential concerns about off-target effects of the system.

result: Photoactivatable Cre offers several advantages: tight control of recombinase activity (photocaging group completely blocks activity, photoactivation generates highly efficient wildtype Cre), ability to remove photocaged amino acid after activation (leaving worms devoid of photocaged Cre), and compatibility with visible light imaging/optogenetics due to photocaging group stability at longer wavelengths.
evaluation: Claims C73-C76 are supported by experimental observations (C73, C74) and citations to prior work (C75) or knowledge of photocaging group chemistry (C76). The tight control is demonstrated by the lack of background activity and high activation efficiency. The compatibility with visible light is a chemical property of the photocaging group.

result: LaserTAC is fast, easily enables preparation of dozens of animals, requires only standard equipment (microscope-mounted laser modified to emit 365 nm), involves straightforward transgenic strain generation, allows investigation of any combination of neurons targeted by a promoter, removes the requirement for creating large numbers of lines, and offers precise temporal control not available with promoter-based systems.
evaluation: Claims C77-C82 describe the practical advantages and versatility of the LaserTAC method. C77 is supported by the authors' experience (DATA). C78-C79 describe technical requirements (KNOWLEDGE). C80-C82 are reasonable inferences about the method's versatility based on its design. The claims about ease of use and versatility are supported by the successful demonstration of the method in the paper.

result: Future applications of the method include controlling expression of endogenous proteins at single-cell resolution using CRISPR/Cas9 to insert loxP sites. The components are functional in other C. elegans tissues and other model systems, suggesting broad applicability beyond the nervous system and beyond C. elegans.
evaluation: Claim C83 is speculative about future applications using CRISPR/Cas9. Claim C84 is supported by citation to prior work (Greiss and Chin, 2011) showing functionality in other tissues. Claim C85 is speculative about broad applicability, though the reasoning is sound given the demonstrated functionality in multiple systems. These represent reasonable expectations for future work but are not demonstrated in this study.
